Cross‑entropy (CE) is chosen as the training loss for large language models because it is the negative log‑likelihood of the true next token, which is smooth and differentiable and therefore works well with gradient‑based optimisation [2].  CE directly rewards the model for assigning high probability to the correct token (lower loss) and penalises it when it assigns high probability to an incorrect token (higher loss) [2][1].

When the model is very confident about a wrong token, the CE loss becomes large.  Since the loss is ‑log of the predicted probability of the true token, a low probability for the correct token (caused by a high probability given to a wrong token) yields a high loss value [1][3].  For example, a prediction that puts 0.84 on the wrong word “fish” gives a loss of ‑log 0.16 ≈ 0.82, which is much higher than a more uncertain “I don’t know” prediction that spreads probability evenly (loss ≈ 0.60) [3].  Thus CE heavily penalises confident but incorrect predictions.
rows.reference: Cross-entropy loss is the negative log-likelihood of the true next token. It is smooth and differentiable, so it suits gradient-based optimisation. The more confident the model is on the correct token, the lower the loss; a confident but wrong prediction is punished hardest (in the slide's example, 0.84 on the wrong token gives a loss of 0.82, worse than the 0.60 for an 'I don't know' uniform prediction).

Perplexity is a measure of a model’s own uncertainty about its next‑token predictions – it can be read as the average number of plausible options the model considers per token, with lower values indicating a more confident (less uncertain) model [5].

\[
\text{PPL}= \exp(\text{cross‑entropy loss}),
\]

Chunk size is a trade-off with a sweet spot
Illustrative: tiny chunks split the answer across many pieces; huge chunks dilute each vector with off-topic text. Recall peaks at a mid size, tune it,

TOP-K / TOP-P
What top-k and top-p actually cut
Same distribution, two rules. Top-k always keeps a fixed number of tokens; top-p keeps however many are needed to reach probability mass p, so
it widens on flat distributions and narrows on confident ones.

What SFT cannot do
▸SFT imitates demonstrations, it copies the answers you show it
▸It has no notion that one answer is better than another, only "this is the target"
▸So it can't directly optimise for helpfulness, safety, or a preferred style
▸For that we need preference and reinforcement methods, the next section

§5 · ENCODERS
Bi-encoder vs. cross-encoder
ADVANCED
Bi-encoder (the vector DB)
• Chunk and query embedded separately
• Embeddings precomputed, query-
independent
• Similarity = cosine of two fixed vectors
• Very fast; scales to millions of chunks
Cross-encoder (the re-ranker)
• Chunk + query fed in together (Sent A +
Sent B)
• Joint attention over the pair at query time
• Outputs one context-dependent relevance
score
• Much slower, score every candidate at
query time

§5 · WHY IT HELPS
Why re-ranking beats plain cosine
▸The vector DB embedded each chunk when it was loaded, before any query existed
▸Those chunk embeddings do not take the user query into account, no Attention over the pair
▸A re-ranker feeds the chunk AND the query to a transformer together
▸It computes a joint, context-dependent similarity score, a far more relevant ranking

§5 · THE FUNNEL
Retrieve wide, then narrow with a cross-encoder
Illustrative: a large, cheap candidate set from the bi-encoder is re-scored by a cross-encoder that reads the query with each chunk, leaving a small,
accurately-ordered top-k for the prompt.

§4 · SIMILARITY
Cosine similarity
▸We often want the document most similar to a user's query (a search engine's core task)
▸Two vectors are similar when they have a large dot (scalar) product
▸But the dot product grows with vector length, longer counts inflate the score
▸Cosine similarity is the normalized dot product: it measures the angle, not the magnitude

rows.response: A cross‑encoder scores each chunk together with the query, allowing the transformer to attend to both inputs and compute a joint, context‑dependent similarity. Because the chunk embeddings used by a bi‑encoder are pre‑computed without any knowledge of the query, they cannot capture how the query relates to each chunk. The cross‑encoder’s joint attention therefore yields a far more relevant ranking than the query‑independent cosine similarity over stored embeddings【2】. Additionally, the cross‑encoder outputs a single relevance score for each pair, whereas cosine similarity only measures the angle between two fixed vectors that were created before the query existed【1】.
rows.reference: The vector database embedded each chunk when it was loaded, before any query existed, so those embeddings do not take the query into account. A cross-encoder feeds the chunk and the query into a transformer together, with joint attention over the pair, and outputs a context-dependent relevance score, which gives a far more relevant ranking. It is much slower, because every candidate must be scored at query time.
